title: Four steps
hookLine: Maimonides: recognize it, regret it, confess it, resolve not to repeat it (Laws of Repentance 2)
carry: sorrow aimed at changing the future

cards: Some apologies have the shape of an apology and almost none of the inside. Sorry you feel that way. Mistakes were made.
A quick sorry tossed over the shoulder on the way out. The difference is easy to hear, even when it's hard to say what's missing.
Moses Maimonides, a rabbi, doctor and philosopher, wrote a code of Jewish law, and inside it a section called the Laws of Repentance.
There he takes yesterday's return and lays it out step by step, so you can see what's missing.

teach.b: First, recognize it. You stop doing the thing, and you see it for what it was. Not a misunderstanding, not bad luck.
A wrong, with your name on it.
Second, regret it. Maimonides wants more than a shrug: the person regrets what they did, looking back and feeling sorry it happened. Sorrow about the past, aimed at changing the future.
Third, confess it. The confession is spoken, said in words, out loud before God. A wrong said out loud, as a sentence, is harder to blur.

Fourth, resolve. You decide not to do it again, and he says the commitment should be real enough that the One who knows the heart could vouch for it. Then he gives a test for when the return is complete.

teach.h: THE SAME CHANCE, AND YOU DON'T.
teach.b: The same situation comes back: the same chance, the same strength, the same temptation. And this time the person doesn't do it, because they've changed, not because they couldn't. And one sharp image.

Confessing without resolving to stop, Maimonides says, is like going into a purifying bath while still holding the very thing that made you impure. The water can't help while your hand is closed around it.
These four steps, in his telling, are between a person and God. When the wrong was done to another person, there's something more, and that's tomorrow.

how: Jews who follow Maimonides' teaching on teshuvah include a spoken confession, called viduy, in prayer, especially on Yom Kippur, alongside regret and a resolve to change.

o: apologize, explain, move on, and try to forget it
feel guilty, keep quiet, and hope it fades away
recognize, regret, confess aloud, resolve not to repeat

p: see the wrong for what it was
decide not to do it again

s: for Maimonides, confession can stay silent, in the head
he says the confession is spoken, in words.
Maimonides tests a complete return by the same situation coming back
the same chance and strength, and this time the person doesn't do it.
confessing while still holding on to the wrong is enough
his image: bathing to purify while still holding what made you impure.

games.q: you've recognized it, regretted it, and confessed it. what is the step Maimonides still asks for?
o: a resolve not to do it again.
games.why: the fourth step is resolve, and he tests it: the same chance comes back, and this time the person doesn't do it.

practice: Choose something small and real from this week, not the worst thing you've ever done, and walk it through the four steps: name it plainly, without excuses; feel its weight for a breath or two, no more; say it in a single whispered sentence, to God if you pray; and decide what you'll do when the same moment comes.
Then breathe out, and let your hands open in your lap.

wordCard.voice: Four steps. Maimonides' shape for teshuvah: recognize it, regret it, confess it, resolve not to repeat it. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: confession, the spoken step in Maimonides' account of teshuvah.

carryVoice: Your line: sorrow aimed at changing the future. The test is the same chance, and a different choice. Day nine hundred forty-one, done.
